extracted.intended_audience: writers and designers of branching narratives / interactive fiction and role-playing game writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical guidelines for designing branching narratives (choose-your-own-adventure, interactive fiction, RPG storylines) that give players meaningful choices while keeping the story manageable and coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan endings and prune branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan the endings where you want people to go and prune possibilities so they don’t multiply out of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every binary decision can split into many realities; without pruning you’ll become overwhelmed. Decide early what endings and early failures you need, prune choices that aren’t needed or sane for your scope, and explicitly mark which choices will be removed or swapped out. Example phrasing from the episode: 'you need to kind of prune it, to make sure it fits the kind of format that feels both dynamic and elegant.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intersections/checkpoints to keep story on track
rubrics_metrics.description: Create checkpoints where diverging paths converge again so you can direct players toward the main story beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design branch points as links in a chain so paths can diverge and then bend back toward intersections. Example: whether players talk to the witch or the dragon, both paths converge on 'Bigfoot’s lair' so the story proceeds as intended. Checkpoints let you let players choose while still guiding them to necessary plot nodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie major story or character beats to convergence points
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure crucial plot or character development happens at nodes where all paths re-converge, or else implement it separately on each path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must hit a key beat for the story, either place it at a checkpoint every path reaches, or reproduce that beat in each branch (which is labor-intensive). The hosts: 'tie the big story beats ... to your checkpoints' and warn that duplicating beats across branches is 'expensive.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Make choices meaningful (not cosmetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Players’ choices should have real consequences rather than being superficial or purely aesthetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choices that only change appearance or give trivial rewards (the 'hat economy'). The best reward is consequences; a change in NPC attitude, available locations, or story outcomes is more meaningful than a cosmetic item. Example: 'When you present a choice to a character, what they get needs to be more than just a hat.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance value across exclusive branches
rubrics_metrics.description: If one branch includes exclusive important information or beat, other branches must give something of equal value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Players don’t mind missing some content if the alternative path offers equally consequential material. Quote: 'If you’re insistent on ... keeping it exclusive for one node, the other node should have information of equal value and consequence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use branches within branches for depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Layer branches (sub-branches) to create richer, nested choices and interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small nested chains (e.g., a long dialogue tree while talking to an NPC) can add depth without exploding global complexity. Example: while talking to the witch who leads to Bigfoot, include a whole subsection about coaxing her into discussing her backstory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make NPCs feel like people via responses and loops
rubrics_metrics.description: Give NPCs reactive dialogue, progressive responses, or looping jokes to make them feel person-like rather than information dispensers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include progressive, silly answers that change over repeated asks until the NPC shuts the chain off (example: prosthetic-limb gag looping 50–60 times then ending). NPCs remembering and reacting to prior choices builds character and verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conditionals and callbacks to show consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Tag player choices so later scenes are altered in small ways that reflect past decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditionals/callbacks are a cheap, low-cost way to make choices feel consequential: a single changed line of dialogue or an NPC reaction on re-encounter can signal lasting impact. Example: insult the witch early, and later she remembers and dislikes you — one line of dialogue conveys consequence without branching complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hat economies (cosmetic-only rewards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reward choices only with cosmetics or items that have no story impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cosmetic rewards (hats/outfits) do not affect the narrative; they feel like empty choices. The hosts emphasize that what players get should change the story/game in meaningful ways, otherwise the choice lacks weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave interpretive space in dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft lines that allow players to bring their own interpretation rather than being overly explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write dialogue that is character-driven but ambiguous enough for players to read into it depending on their emotional state; avoid directive lines that remove player interpretation (e.g., prefer 'Is that the choice you’re making?' over 'I wouldn’t make that choice if I were you'). Actor delivery can add layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use objectives/items to create apparent freedom while guiding players
rubrics_metrics.description: Design required objectives or item mechanics so players feel free but are still funneled through designed encounters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a castle infiltration where players can choose many approaches but still must obtain a key in the Queen’s chamber; even if they get to the vault early, a required item forces them to visit designed areas. This preserves player agency while ensuring they encounter intended content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use access as consequence to control direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Lock or unlock access to areas or layers of the story as a consequence of choices to direct pacing and progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving access to the next layer (e.g., Shadow Point Observatory example) feels like a meaningful reward and can channel players toward desired content while offering multiple paths to earn that access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline branch structure visually (flowcharts/maps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create visual maps or flowcharts of branching paths to understand divergence and reconvergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study choose-your-own-adventure plot maps or subway-map-like diagrams to help plan pruning and checkpoints; visualizing the tree aids sanity and design decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide which pieces cannot be pruned and which can be reused
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine ahead of time which nodes are essential and which can be removed or repurposed; plan asset reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify non-prunable story pieces you must keep. For disposable elements, plan to file 'serial numbers off' NPCs and reuse dialogue/clothing/other assets in other nodes to save work. This helps manage content creation cost and maintain coherence when players make unexpected choices.
